articleTitle: Energy storage in rotating machines
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The author discusses energy storage in three forms of rotating machines: flywheels, homopolar generators, and compulsators (compensated pulsed alternators). The disadvantages of flywheels and homopolar generators are discussed. The requirements for shorter pulses are met by compulsators in which compensating currents reduce the armature inductance. The three methods of producing compensation, active, passive, and selectively passive, are discussed in detail.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Measurement of induced current in loaded loop antennas
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: Classical formulations of coupling theory are based on narrow band, steady state, frequency domain techniques, with consideration given mainly to linear loads and small signal analyses. For high voltage, short pulse coupling such theories become difficult to use. The authors outline an alternative method of analysis and measurement based on integral solutions of Maxwell's equations in the time domain. The authors use the integral equation formulation to consider the important case of coupling to loop structures and present experimental and theoretical results for the current induced in circular loops loaded by linear and nonlinear loads. They are specifically interested in coupling to electrically large loops, which in the time domain implies pulse lengths of the order of or less than loop diameter. The main motivation for this work is to assess the coupling of subnanosecond pulses to loops on printed circuit boards designed for use in computer and control systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Progress on Mogul E-a flash radiograph facility
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: Summary form only given. Mogul E, a flash radiographic machine was designed by the Pulse Power Group at AWE(A). It is now under construction and should be completed by the end of 1992. It will be an 11 MV and 65 ns X-ray generator, accelerating a 35 kA electron beam of diameter less than 1 cm to impinge on a thin tantalum target. The device consists of an 84 stage 0.7 mu F 100 kV capacitor stack Marx generator driving a 45 Omega Blumlein pulse forming transmission line circuit.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: High power, high repetition rate switches: an overview
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: All directed energy concepts require a pulsed power system to operate. Several of the systems considered must operate repetitively. Currents in the range of kA to MA, voltages in the range of kV to MV, repetition rates of 10 Hz to 100 kHz, and pulse widths of 100 nanoseconds to 100 milliseconds, are reasonable requirements. The author discusses some of the research on high power switching technology with the emphasis on opening switches. The requirements and types of switch are briefly discussed and then the development trends of three switches are described. The three switches are plasma switches, gas discharge switches, and solid state switches.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Inductive energy storage and homopolar generators
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The pulse power requirements for an electromagnetic railgun depend primarily on the energy required for the projectile, the time of flight in the railgun barrel, and the barrel efficiency. One of the most usual railgun power sources is the DC homopolar generator (HPG). A major shortcoming of the HPG is that it produces a low EMF (usually little more than 100 V) and it cannot therefore deliver the required power directly to the rails. Instead the HPG is used with a suitable inductor which acts as an intermediate energy store (IES). The inductor will usually be charged over a period of 100-200 milliseconds (the rise time) and then rapidly discharged into the rails (barrel time) so as to produce the required voltage for projectile acceleration. There are two types of inductor, solenoidal and toroidal. The author describes toroidal inductors, which are air-cored, for use with HPG. The key parameters of the inductors are discussed. These are: resistance, stray field impacts, EM stresses in the coil, and the skin effect.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Solid state switching devices
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The author briefly discusses the improvements in power semiconductor switches resulting from new power thyristor designs, in particular gate turn-off thyristors. A special variant of the GTO, the zero turn-off thyristor optimised for high di/dt, high peak current requirements, are mentioned. The status of power semiconductor thyristors and future trends concerning pulsed power applications are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Ignitrons for new applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The ignitron is a suitable tube for many pulse power applications. It is being used in an increasing number of research and industrial applications. It can be used in series and/or parallel to extend it's capability. The author discusses three applications of ignitrons: as crowbar protection for travelling wave tubes, to ensure voltage hold-off reliability in rail gun power sources, and food processing industry applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Diagnostics of high-power microwave and millimetre-wave pulses
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The measurement of pulsed power flow from a Marx generator into a vacuum diode load and the subsequent measurement of the radiated microwave and millimetre-wave pulsed power, has needed the use of some existing and new diagnostic techniques. The research programme has been concerned with the design, construction, operation and assessment of a series of pulsed cold-cathode electron cyclotron masers. The author discusses the diagnostic techniques for frequency, power, and mode type.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Capacitor technology
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The use of capacitors as an energy storage medium is well established and generally considered the most satisfactory means of utilising electrical energy in certain applications. Capacitors can release their energy at extremely high speed and, when the associated charging equipment and load requires, at a very high repetition rate. These capacitors are capable of producing high peak currents at many kV unlike other forms of energy storage systems. Capacitor technology for pulsed power applications has seen significant changes. The main areas are dielectric materials, energy density levels and control of voltage reversal. The author briefly discusses each of these areas as well as the repetition rate of discharges.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Magnetic materials for pulsed power
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The author briefly discusses the varied uses of magnetic materials in pulsed power applications, in particular magnetic pulse compression. The requirements of magnetic materials for such applications are described. Magnetic pulse sharpening is also discussed as is the use of magnetic materials in the conversion of chemically stored energy (explosives) into electricity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Recent advances in thyratron design
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The task of thyratron design and manufacture has advanced the capabilities of the thyratron significantly. These advances depend not only on the ability to examine a specific set of operating parameters and tailor the thyratron to meet those requirements, but also on the ability to design and construct circuits for the purposes of testing. The motivation for development of new thyratrons is, almost without exception, driven entirely by specific application requirements, and this, as a matter of necessity, usually entails a short development turn-around time. The author describes some examples of thyratron developments which have required enhancement of various combinations of the following parameters: recovery time; operating voltage; rate of rise of current; average power; peak power; repetition rate; inductance (i.e. length of device); and immunity to capacitive triggering. The author gives four examples: the CX1725, a double-gap hollow-anode thyratron; the CX2025, a four-gap thyratron; the CX2024, also four gap; and the CX1836 for which the author discusses immunity to capacitive triggering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experience with using Rogowski coils for transient measurements
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: Rogowski coils have been used for detection and low-accuracy measurement of electric currents for decades. They are now the preferred method of current measurement for a whole range of measurements and investigations because they have more suitable features than current transformers and other iron-cored devices. A Rogowski coil is basically a toroidal winding placed round the conductor to be measured. The output from the winding is an EMF proportional to the rate of change of current. The coils are designed to give a high degree of rejection to external magnetic fields.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A long life, 2 kHz X-ray preioniser
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: Progress towards achieving kilohertz repetition rate, kilowatt class excimer lasers has spurred the development of long life, high repetition rate X-ray preionisers. An X-ray preioniser has three main parts-driver, cathodes and anode. In its simplest form there are two electrodes separated by a dielectric surface and a fast rising voltage pulse across these produces a corona emission. This discharge spreads out, desorbing and removing surface material which is ionised and in this way a surface plasma is formed. The construction and operation of an X-ray preioniser is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design, control and fault protection of resonant charging circuits for high frequency laser pulse modulators
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: Current research on pulsed gas lasers operating in the high mean power, multikilohertz regime has resulted in a resurgence in the development of HV pulse modulators. With few exceptions the pulse modulators employ one or more capacitive storage networks which provide excitation pulses of the correct duration, amplitude and impedance when discharged into the laser cavity. The author discusses the practical design of such HV charging systems, with reference to the development of a charging state employed in an 88 kW mean power excimer laser charging circuit.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Photoconductive power switches
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: Photoconductive switches offer potential advantages over conventional pulsed power switches which can be summarized briefly as follows: optical trigger isolation, low inductance, short risetime, short recovery time, scalability to high voltages and/or currents, operation at high repetition rates and light weight. These properties make photoconductive power switches attractive for various applications such as impulse radar or RF weapons. The author presents an introduction into photoconductive switches, including a comparison of three semiconductor materials (Si, GaAs and diamond) used for switching and a description of some of the GaAs photoconductive switching conducted at the Sowerby Research Centre.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer simulations of charged particle motion in pulsed fields
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: Static or moving charged particles are successfully incorporated in a transmission line model for numerical electromagnetic field computations based on a two-dimensional series connected node. The approach is validated by applying it to a simple vacuum diode for which analytical results can be obtained. The time-domain nature of the transmission line approach makes the new computer program developed ideal for simulating pulsed power phenomena and devices.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The electro-magnetic launcher facility at Kirkcudbright
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: The authors look at the design and construction of the new electromagnetic launcher facility at Kirkcudbright for the joint UK-US development programme into EM launch technology. The facility uses 32 MJ 11 kV capacitive storage for pulsed power which is based on the Thunderbolt system in the USA. The launcher and monitoring systems are described in less detail.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The MAGPIE project: current status (generator for plasma implosions)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: A mega-ampere generator for plasma implosion experiments (MAGPIE) is being constructed at Imperial College, London. The MAGPIE generator design consists of four separate Marx banks, each connected to a coaxial, water filled, transmission line and a switch. Each Marx bank consists of 24100 kV, 0.7 mu F capacitors arranged in a bipolar charging configuration, giving an output of 2.4 MV with a stored energy of 86 kJ. The generator is specifically designed to enable radiative collapse experiments to be carried out in a hydrogen fibre dense 2-pinch.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of a 100 kV sub-nanosecond rise-time pulser to material testing
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Pulsed Power Technology
abstract: For some years the High Voltage Laboratory at City University has had a 100 kV cable pulser with a pulse rise time of less than 0.3 nanoseconds. The 100 kV high value charging resistor protects the DC charging source from being shorted when the pulser operates. The 100 kV 50 ohm charging cable is connected through a switch and then by a very short cable to the co-axial test cell and its matching resistor. Materials tested in the cell could be liquids or surge diverter blocks, etc., where it is important to be able to calculate the resistance-voltage characteristic and energy dissipation. The authors describe the method used to obtain this data from the voltage waveform given at the matching resistor attenuator.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
